learningObjectives.title: Elements, compounds and mixtures, and how mixtures are separated
Particles in motion: states of matter and changes of state
Temperature measures average kinetic energy; converting Celsius and kelvin
Counting protons, neutrons and electrons from the nuclear symbol
Isotopes and relative atomic mass from abundances
How atoms emit light, and what colour, wavelength and energy mean
What the hydrogen spectrum proves about energy levels
How many electrons each main level can hold
Sublevels and the shapes of s and p orbitals
Writing electron configurations with Aufbau, Pauli and Hund
From the convergence limit to ionization energy, and the trends in it
Reading successive ionization energies for the group

questions.q: Which substance is a compound, and for the correct reason?
options: Oxygen, since each of its molecules contains two atoms bonded together
Air, since it contains several elements in the same proportions everywhere
Carbon dioxide, since it contains atoms of two elements bonded in a fixed ratio
Salt water, since the salt and the water have combined to form one new substance
optionWhy: A student who equates 'molecule' with 'compound' picks this. O₂ molecules contain two atoms of the SAME element, so oxygen is an element. A compound needs atoms of different elements bonded together.

A student who counts elements, or who reads air's percentages as a fixed formula, picks this. The nitrogen and oxygen in air are separate molecules, not bonded to each other, so air is a mixture; its proportions also vary (water vapour especially).
Carbon dioxide, CO₂, contains carbon and oxygen atoms chemically bonded in a fixed 1:2 ratio, which is what makes a substance a compound.
A student who thinks dissolving is a chemical change picks this. Salt water is a mixture: the salt-to-water ratio can vary and evaporating the water gives back sodium chloride unchanged.
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide, CO₂, contains carbon and oxygen atoms chemically bonded in a fixed 1:2 ratio, which is what makes a substance a compound.

questions.q: Hydrogen and oxygen gases are mixed and ignited. They react to form water. Which statement about the water formed is correct?
options: Its hydrogen and oxygen can be separated again simply by boiling it
Its hydrogen and oxygen are bonded together in a fixed ratio
Its hydrogen and oxygen each keep their own properties
Its hydrogen and oxygen are in whatever ratio of gases was mixed
optionWhy: A student who thinks compounds can be separated by physical methods picks this. Boiling turns water into water vapour, H₂O(g); the molecules stay intact. Separating water into hydrogen and oxygen needs a chemical change, such as electrolysis.

Water is a compound: every H₂O molecule contains hydrogen and oxygen atoms chemically bonded in a 2:1 ratio, so pure water always has the same composition by mass, whatever proportions of the gases were mixed.
A student who thinks the elements keep their properties in a compound picks this. Hydrogen burns and oxygen supports burning; water does neither. A compound has new properties of its own.

A student who thinks a compound's composition depends on the amounts used to make it picks this. Water always contains hydrogen and oxygen atoms in a 2:1 ratio; if more of one gas is mixed, the excess is left over unreacted, not built into the water.
questions.explain: Water is a compound: every H₂O molecule contains hydrogen and oxygen atoms chemically bonded in a 2:1 ratio, so pure water always has the same composition by mass, whatever proportions of the gases were mixed.

questions.q: Which statement about the vaporization of water is correct?
options: Evaporation can take place only once the water has reached its boiling point
Evaporation takes place at the surface, even well below the boiling point
The large bubbles in boiling water contain hydrogen and oxygen
The large bubbles in boiling water are air from the gaps between the particles
optionWhy: A student who confuses evaporation with boiling picks this. Evaporation happens from the surface at any temperature; only boiling requires the boiling point.

Water particles have a range of kinetic energies. At any temperature some particles at the surface have enough energy to overcome the attractions and escape, which is why puddles dry at 20 °C. Boiling, with bubbles of vapour throughout the liquid, happens at the boiling point.

A student who thinks boiling splits water into its elements picks this. The bubbles contain water vapour, H₂O(g). Boiling overcomes the attractions between water molecules; the covalent bonds within them are unchanged.
A student who thinks there is air between particles picks this. The space between particles is empty. The large bubbles that form throughout boiling water contain water vapour, H₂O(g).
questions.explain: Water particles have a range of kinetic energies. At any temperature some particles at the surface have enough energy to overcome the attractions and escape, which is why puddles dry at 20 °C. Boiling, with bubbles of vapour throughout the liquid, happens at the boiling point.

questions.q: A molecular solid, X, is heated at a constant rate. Its temperature rises to 80 °C, stays at 80 °C for six minutes while the solid melts, and then rises again. Which explains why the temperature stays constant while X melts?
options: The energy supplied is lost to the surroundings, so X absorbs none of it as it melts
The energy absorbed overcomes attractions between molecules; their average Ek is constant
The energy absorbed breaks the covalent bonds within each of the molecules of X
The energy absorbed is used to make each molecule expand as the solid melts
optionWhy: A student who thinks energy absorbed must always raise the temperature concludes that a flat section means the energy is not reaching X. X does absorb energy at a constant rate while it melts; the energy overcomes the attractions between molecules instead of increasing their average kinetic energy, so the temperature stays constant.

Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles. While X melts, the energy absorbed separates the molecules against their attractions, so the average kinetic energy, and the temperature, stay constant until all the solid has melted.
A student who thinks melting breaks the bonds within molecules picks this. Melting overcomes the attractions between molecules; the covalent bonds are unchanged, so the liquid is still X.

A student who gives molecules the properties of the bulk substance picks this. Molecules do not expand or melt; melting is a change in how the molecules are arranged and move, as the attractions between them are overcome.
questions.explain: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles. While X melts, the energy absorbed separates the molecules against their attractions, so the average kinetic energy, and the temperature, stay constant until all the solid has melted.

questions.q: Which statement about temperature is correct?
options: A temperature of 0 K is the same as a temperature of 273 °C
Doubling a temperature in °C doubles the average kinetic energy
A rise of 1 K is exactly the same size as a rise of 1 °C
Temperature in K measures how much heat a sample holds
optionWhy: A student who always adds 273 when converting picks this. To convert kelvin to Celsius, subtract 273: 0 K = −273 °C, absolute zero.

A student who takes average kinetic energy to be proportional to the Celsius temperature picks this. It is proportional to the temperature in kelvin: 20 °C (293 K) to 40 °C (313 K) raises it by only about 7%.
The kelvin has the same incremental value as the Celsius degree; the two scales differ only in their zero (0 K = −273 °C). So a temperature change of 25 °C is a change of 25 K.

A student who treats temperature and heat as the same picks this. Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles and does not depend on the size of the sample; heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference.
questions.explain: The kelvin has the same incremental value as the Celsius degree; the two scales differ only in their zero (0 K = −273 °C). So a temperature change of 25 °C is a change of 25 K.

questions.q: Which statement about the nucleus of an atom is correct?
options: It takes up most of the atom's volume, with electrons at its surface.
Its density is far greater than the average density of the atom.
It contains only about two-thirds of the mass of the atom.
It contains the electrons as well as the protons and neutrons.
optionWhy: Textbook diagrams draw the nucleus as a large ball, but they are not to scale. The nucleus is roughly 10 000 to 100 000 times smaller in diameter than the atom; the electrons occupy almost all of the atom's volume.

Correct. Nearly all of the atom's mass is in the nucleus, because electrons are so light. The nucleus is of order 10⁻¹⁵ m across and the atom of order 10⁻¹⁰ m, so the nucleus occupies only about (10⁻¹⁵ ÷ 10⁻¹⁰)³ = 10⁻¹⁵ of the atom's volume. Nearly all the mass in a tiny volume makes the nucleus extremely dense.

If electrons were as heavy as protons, an atom with similar numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons would carry about a third of its mass outside the nucleus. In fact an electron's relative mass is about 0.0005, compared with 1 for a proton or neutron, so electrons contribute a negligible fraction and nearly all of the mass is in the nucleus.
The nucleus contains only nucleons: protons and neutrons. The electrons occupy the space outside the nucleus.
questions.explain: Correct. Nearly all of the atom's mass is in the nucleus, because electrons are so light. The nucleus is of order 10⁻¹⁵ m across and the atom of order 10⁻¹⁰ m, so the nucleus occupies only about (10⁻¹⁵ ÷ 10⁻¹⁰)³ = 10⁻¹⁵ of the atom's volume. Nearly all the mass in a tiny volume makes the nucleus extremely dense.

questions.q: Two atoms have the same atomic number but different mass numbers. Which statement about these atoms is correct?
options: They belong to different elements, as they contain different numbers of nucleons in total.
They belong to the same element, as they differ only in their numbers of neutrons.
They have different numbers of electrons, as their mass numbers are different.
They undergo different chemical reactions, because their atoms have different masses.
optionWhy: The element is fixed by the number of protons, not by the number of nucleons. The same atomic number means the same element; the extra nucleons are neutrons.
Correct. The atomic number (number of protons) defines the element. Different mass numbers with the same atomic number mean different numbers of neutrons: the atoms are isotopes of one element.

Neutral atoms have as many electrons as protons, and both atoms have the same atomic number, so they have the same number of electrons. A different number of electrons would make an ion, not an isotope.
Chemical reactions depend on electrons, and isotopes have the same number and arrangement of electrons, so they undergo the same reactions. Only mass-dependent physical properties differ.
questions.explain: Correct. The atomic number (number of protons) defines the element. Different mass numbers with the same atomic number mean different numbers of neutrons: the atoms are isotopes of one element.

questions.q: Chlorine (atomic number 17) has isotopes with mass numbers 35 and 37. Pure samples of ³⁵Cl₂ gas and ³⁷Cl₂ gas are compared at the same temperature and pressure. Which statement is correct?
options: The ³⁷Cl₂ gas diffuses more slowly than ³⁵Cl₂.
The two gases diffuse at the same rate as each other.
The two gases undergo different chemical reactions.
The ³⁷Cl₂ molecules contain more electrons than ³⁵Cl₂.
optionWhy: Correct. At the same temperature the molecules of both gases have the same mean kinetic energy, so the heavier ³⁷Cl₂ molecules move more slowly on average and the gas diffuses more slowly. Rate of diffusion is a physical property that differs between isotopes.

Isotopes have the same chemical properties, but not the same physical properties. ³⁷Cl₂ molecules (relative mass about 74) are heavier than ³⁵Cl₂ molecules (about 70), so at the same temperature they move more slowly and diffuse more slowly.

Both isotopes have 17 electrons with the same arrangement, so ³⁵Cl₂ and ³⁷Cl₂ undergo the same chemical reactions. The difference between them is in mass-dependent physical properties such as rate of diffusion.
Every chlorine atom has 17 electrons whatever its mass number, so both molecules contain 34 electrons. The isotopes differ in their numbers of neutrons (18 and 20).
questions.explain: Correct. At the same temperature the molecules of both gases have the same mean kinetic energy, so the heavier ³⁷Cl₂ molecules move more slowly on average and the gas diffuses more slowly. Rate of diffusion is a physical property that differs between isotopes.

questions.q: The mass spectrum of element E shows three peaks from singly charged atomic ions: m/z 24 (relative abundance 100), m/z 25 (relative abundance 12.7) and m/z 26 (relative abundance 13.9). What is the relative atomic mass of E, calculated from these data?
optionWhy: Dividing the weighted sum 3078.9 by 100 treats the relative abundances as percentages, but they add up to 126.6. A_r must lie between 24 and 26; 30.79 is outside that range.
24 is the m/z of the tallest peak, the most abundant isotope. The other two isotopes also contribute, so A_r is a weighted mean that lies a little above 24.
25 is the simple mean of 24, 25 and 26, which would be correct only if the three isotopes were equally abundant. The isotope with m/z 24 is far more abundant, so each value must be weighted.

questions.q: The mass spectrum of a sample of copper shows two peaks from singly charged atomic ions: m/z 63 (relative abundance 100) and m/z 65 (relative abundance 44.6). What do these peaks show?
options: The sample also contains a second element, of mass 65.
The A_r of copper is 63, which is the m/z of the tallest peak.
The A_r of copper is 64, the mean of the two m/z values.
Copper atoms exist with two numbers of neutrons, 34 and 36.
optionWhy: Atoms of one element can have different masses: these are isotopes. Different mass numbers do not mean different elements; the element is fixed by the number of protons.
The tallest peak gives the mass of the most abundant isotope, copper-63. A_r is the weighted mean of both peaks: (63 × 100 + 65 × 44.6) ÷ 144.6 = 63.62 from these whole-number values.
64 is the simple mean, correct only if both isotopes were equally abundant. The peak at 63 is more than twice as tall, so A_r lies closer to 63.

Correct. Each peak from singly charged atomic ions corresponds to one isotope. Copper atoms all have the same number of protons, so masses of 63 and 65 mean two different numbers of neutrons (34 and 36).
questions.explain: Correct. Each peak from singly charged atomic ions corresponds to one isotope. Copper atoms all have the same number of protons, so masses of 63 and 65 mean two different numbers of neutrons (34 and 36).

questions.q: When sodium compounds are heated in a flame, the flame turns yellow. Which process in the sodium atoms produces this yellow light?
options: Excited electrons fall to lower energy levels, emitting photons.
Electrons absorb energy and emit photons as they rise to higher levels.
Electrons escape from the atoms entirely, releasing energy as photons.
The hot atoms glow with the yellow colour that sodium atoms possess.
optionWhy: Heat excites electrons to higher energy levels. When they fall back to lower levels, each transition emits a photon whose energy equals the difference between the two levels; the main sodium transitions give yellow light.
Rising to a higher level requires energy to be absorbed, so no photon is emitted in that step. The light is emitted afterwards, when the excited electrons fall back to lower levels.
Removing an electron from an atom is ionization, which requires energy rather than releasing light. The emission lines come from electrons that stay in the atom and fall between its energy levels.
Individual atoms do not have a colour. The yellow is the light emitted as photons of particular energies when excited electrons in sodium atoms fall to lower energy levels.
questions.explain: Heat excites electrons to higher energy levels. When they fall back to lower levels, each transition emits a photon whose energy equals the difference between the two levels; the main sodium transitions give yellow light.

questions.q: Consider the set of lines in the hydrogen emission spectrum produced by electrons falling to n = 2 from higher levels. Which statement about the lines in this set is correct?
options: The lines are equally spaced in frequency across the set.
The lines get closer together towards higher frequency.
The lines get closer together towards lower frequency.
The lines are dark gaps across a continuous band of colour.
optionWhy: Equal spacing would require equally spaced energy levels. The levels get closer together at higher energy, so the lines crowd together towards higher frequency.

The energy levels get closer together as n increases, so the energy differences for falls to n = 2 from n = 3, 4, 5, … increase by ever smaller amounts. The lines therefore converge towards higher frequency.
This would be true only if the levels spread further apart at higher energy. The energy gaps shrink as n increases, so the lines converge at the high-frequency end of the set.
Dark lines on a continuous band form an absorption spectrum. An emission spectrum consists of bright lines, which in each set converge towards higher frequency.
questions.explain: The energy levels get closer together as n increases, so the energy differences for falls to n = 2 from n = 3, 4, 5, … increase by ever smaller amounts. The lines therefore converge towards higher frequency.

questions.q: Which electron transition in a hydrogen atom emits the photon of highest frequency?
optionWhy: This fall spans four levels, but the levels are not equally spaced: the gaps near n = 6 are tiny. The single gap from n = 2 to n = 1 alone is larger than the whole fall from n = 6 to n = 2, so n = 4 → n = 1 gives the higher frequency.

Moving from n = 1 up to n = 5 requires energy to be absorbed; no photon is emitted. Emission happens when an electron falls, and of the falls listed, n = 4 → n = 1 involves the largest energy difference.

The photon’s energy is the difference between the two levels, not the energy of the level the electron lands in. The gap between n = 6 and n = 5 is the smallest here, so this photon has the lowest frequency (it is in the infrared).

Photon energy, and therefore frequency, equals the energy difference between the two levels. Falls to n = 1 involve the largest gaps, because the levels are much further apart near n = 1. The n = 4 → n = 1 fall releases far more energy than 6 → 2 or 6 → 5.
questions.explain: Photon energy, and therefore frequency, equals the energy difference between the two levels. Falls to n = 1 involve the largest gaps, because the levels are much further apart near n = 1. The n = 4 → n = 1 fall releases far more energy than 6 → 2 or 6 → 5.

questions.q: What is the maximum total number of electrons that the first three main energy levels of an atom (n = 1, 2 and 3) can hold?
optionWhy: The '2, 8, 8' pattern describes the first 20 elements, not the capacity of the third level. The third level can hold 2 × 3² = 18 electrons (3s², 3p⁶, 3d¹⁰), so the total is 2 + 8 + 18 = 28.
Level n holds a maximum of 2n² electrons: 2 × 1² = 2, 2 × 2² = 8 and 2 × 3² = 18, giving 2 + 8 + 18 = 28.
1 + 4 + 9 = 14 is the number of orbitals in the first three levels (n² for each). Each orbital holds two electrons of opposite spin, so the capacity is 2n² per level: 2 + 8 + 18 = 28.

Giving each sublevel room for one pair (2, then 2 + 2, then 2 + 2 + 2) treats every sublevel as a single orbital. The p sublevel has three orbitals and the d sublevel five, so the capacities are 2, 8 and 18, totalling 28.
questions.explain: Level n holds a maximum of 2n² electrons: 2 × 1² = 2, 2 × 2² = 8 and 2 × 3² = 18, giving 2 + 8 + 18 = 28.
questions.working: Maximum electrons in level n = 2n². n = 1: 2 × 1² = 2; n = 2: 2 × 2² = 8; n = 3: 2 × 3² = 18. Total = 2 + 8 + 18 = 28.

questions.q: Which description of a 1s atomic orbital is correct?
options: A circular path round the nucleus along which the electron travels at a fixed distance
A spherical region centred on the nucleus that contains the electron at every instant
A spherical region centred on the nucleus where the electron is most likely to be found
A spherical shell with its two electrons held at fixed points on opposite sides of the nucleus
optionWhy: An orbital is not an orbit. The electron does not follow a path; the orbital describes a region, here a sphere, where the electron is likely to be found.
The shape is right, but the drawn sphere encloses a high probability, not certainty. There is a small probability of finding the electron outside it.
An s orbital is spherical and centred on the nucleus. An orbital is a region of space where there is a high probability of finding the electron, not a path or a container.

Electrons are not held at fixed points; that is a shell-diagram drawing convention. The 1s orbital is a spherical region, centred on the nucleus, where there is a high probability of finding its electrons.
questions.explain: An s orbital is spherical and centred on the nucleus. An orbital is a region of space where there is a high probability of finding the electron, not a path or a container.

questions.q: Which condensed electron configuration of a ground-state atom is correct?
options: copper: [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s²
chromium: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹
potassium: [Ar] 3d¹
iron: [Ar] 4s² 4p⁶
optionWhy: This is what the regular filling order predicts, but copper (Z = 29) is the other exception: it is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹.
Chromium (Z = 24) is one of the two exceptions to the simple filling order: it is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹, not [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s².
After 3p the next electron enters 4s, not 3d, because 4s is lower in energy in potassium. Potassium (Z = 19) is [Ar] 4s¹.
The third level is not full at eight electrons; it can hold 18, including ten in 3d. After 4s the next electrons enter 3d, not 4p: iron (Z = 26) is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s².
questions.explain: Chromium (Z = 24) is one of the two exceptions to the simple filling order: it is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹, not [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s².

questions.q: What is the maximum number of electrons that a 3d sublevel can hold, and why?
options: 20 electrons, as its ten orbitals can each hold two electrons of opposite spin
18 electrons, as the n = 3 energy level holds a maximum of 2n² electrons
10 electrons, as its five orbitals can each hold two electrons of opposite spin
2 electrons, as the 3d sublevel is one orbital that holds a single pair
optionWhy: A d sublevel has five orbitals, not ten; ten is its electron capacity. Five orbitals × 2 electrons = 10.
2n² = 18 is the capacity of the whole third main level (3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰), shared among three sublevels. The 3d sublevel alone holds 10.
A d sublevel contains five orbitals, and each orbital holds at most two electrons, which must have opposite spins (the Pauli exclusion principle): 5 × 2 = 10.
The 3d sublevel is not a single orbital; it contains five orbitals. Each holds up to two electrons, so the sublevel holds 10.
questions.explain: A d sublevel contains five orbitals, and each orbital holds at most two electrons, which must have opposite spins (the Pauli exclusion principle): 5 × 2 = 10.
questions.working: A d sublevel has 5 orbitals; each orbital holds a maximum of 2 electrons (opposite spins). Maximum = 5 × 2 = 10 electrons.

questions.q: How does the first ionization energy change from lithium to sodium to potassium in group 1, and why?
options: It decreases, as the outer electron is in a higher main level, further out and more shielded.
It decreases, as the fixed pull of the nucleus is shared among a larger number of electrons.
It increases, as the nuclear charge rises from +3 to +19 and attracts the electron more strongly.
It stays the same, as each atom must lose just one electron to reach a full outer shell.
optionWhy: Down the group the electron removed is in a higher main energy level (n = 2, 3, 4), further from the nucleus and shielded by more inner electrons. This outweighs the rise in nuclear charge, so less energy is needed: Li 520, Na 496, K 419 kJ mol⁻¹.

The trend is right but the reason is not. A nucleus does not have a fixed amount of attraction to share out. The outer electron is held less strongly because it is further from the nucleus and more shielded.
Nuclear charge does rise, but it is not the only factor. The outer electron is much further out and more shielded in potassium, so the first ionization energy falls from 520 to 419 kJ mol⁻¹.

Ionization energy measures how strongly the electron removed is attracted, not how many electrons stand between the atom and a full shell. The outer electron is further out and more shielded down the group, so the value falls.
questions.explain: Down the group the electron removed is in a higher main energy level (n = 2, 3, 4), further from the nucleus and shielded by more inner electrons. This outweighs the rise in nuclear charge, so less energy is needed: Li 520, Na 496, K 419 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: The first four successive ionization energies of an element X are 578, 1817, 2745 and 11 577 kJ mol⁻¹. In which group of the periodic table is X?
options: Group 14, as the large increase appears at the fourth ionization energy
Group 1, as the second value is already over three times larger than the first
Group 13, as the large increase comes after the third electron is removed
Group 3, as exactly three electrons are removed before the large increase occurs
optionWhy: The large value is the fourth, but the number of outer electrons is the number removed BEFORE the jump: three, not four. Three outer electrons (ns² np¹) place X in group 13.
Successive ionization energies always rise. The increase from 2745 to 11 577 is far larger than the earlier rises, so the jump comes after the third electron: group 13.

The rises from 578 to 1817 to 2745 are steady, then the fourth value is about four times the third. Three electrons are removed before the big jump, so X has three outer electrons (ns² np¹): group 13. X is aluminium.
Three outer electrons is correct, but in the 1–18 numbering a p-block element with three outer electrons is in group 13. Group 3 is a d-block group (scandium, yttrium).
questions.explain: The rises from 578 to 1817 to 2745 are steady, then the fourth value is about four times the third. Three electrons are removed before the big jump, so X has three outer electrons (ns² np¹): group 13. X is aluminium.

questions.q: The graph shows log₁₀ of the successive ionization energies of an element plotted against the number of electrons removed. In which group of the periodic table is the element?
options: Group 14, because the first large jump comes after four electrons have been removed
Group 15, because the first large jump is seen at the fifth ionization energy
Group 12, because the largest jump on the graph comes after the twelfth electron
Group 4, because four electrons are removed before the first large jump
optionWhy: The values rise steadily for the first four electrons and then jump sharply at the fifth, so four electrons are removed from the outer level before an inner level (n = 2) is reached. Four outer electrons (ns² np²) place the element in group 14; the second jump after the twelfth electron marks the n = 1 level, so the element is silicon.
The fifth ionization energy is the first high value, but it is the number of electrons removed BEFORE the jump that counts: four. Four outer electrons mean group 14, not 15.

The jump after the twelfth electron marks the start of the n = 1 level, not the end of the outer electrons. It is the FIRST large jump, after the fourth electron, that shows how many outer electrons there are: four, so group 14.

Four outer electrons is the right reading of the graph, but in the 1–18 numbering a p-block element with four outer electrons (ns² np²) is in group 14. Group 4 is a d-block group (titanium, zirconium).
questions.explain: The values rise steadily for the first four electrons and then jump sharply at the fifth, so four electrons are removed from the outer level before an inner level (n = 2) is reached. Four outer electrons (ns² np²) place the element in group 14; the second jump after the twelfth electron marks the n = 1 level, so the element is silicon.
questions.working: Read the graph: the points rise gently for electrons 1–4, then jump between the 4th and 5th values (the first large jump). Four electrons are removed before the jump, so the element has four outer electrons (ns² np²): group 14. The second jump between the 12th and 13th values marks the two n = 1 electrons, so the element has 14 electrons in total and is silicon.
